name: Borage (starflower) seed oil
short: Case report: status epilepticus after 1 week of use. Eczema: fairly common, mild, mainly gut effects, as with placebo. Arthritis, 3 oils pooled incl. borage: adverse events 20% vs 3%, not significant.
text: A case report describes status epilepticus (prolonged seizures) in a patient who had taken borage oil by mouth for one week. A Cochrane review of 27 randomised trials of oral evening primrose oil or borage oil for eczema (8 of them on borage oil) found that both oils had the same fairly common, mild, transient adverse effects as their placebos, mainly gastrointestinal, but the short-term trials did not examine possible adverse effects of long-term use; the review's other cautions, a case report of possible inflammation, thrombosis and immunosuppression with use for more than a year and a study suggesting increased bleeding in people taking warfarin, concern evening primrose oil, not borage oil. In a Cochrane review of rheumatoid arthritis trials that pooled gamma-linolenic acid from evening primrose, borage or blackcurrant seed oil, adverse events occurred in 20% with these oils versus 3% with placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant; the abstract does not give figures for borage oil alone. The safety of borage has been questioned because the plant contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which are known for liver toxicity, but a systematic review of case reports of possible pyrrolizidine alkaloid harm from borage, coltsfoot or comfrey found none involving borage, and a laboratory analysis of one commercial borage seed oil found that any pyrrolizidine alkaloids present were below 200 parts per trillion, noting earlier studies showing these alkaloids are not co-extracted with the oil. No interaction data on borage oil itself were found in the cited sources.
